items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman / Bloomberg)
items.title: France-Germany 10y at 141bp: widest since the 2012 crisis, and Italy's 2y spread nearly doubled in one session
items.idea: OAT-Bund 10y closed 14bp wider at 141bp, the widest since the sovereign-debt crisis. Italy-Germany 2y nearly doubled to 55bp, the biggest one-day closing jump since 2020; the French 2y spread blew out as much as 22bp, the most since 2012. French CDS has more than doubled in a month. Growth isn't the story: Goldman's current-quarter tracker has sat near 0.1% for a month.
items.angle: Spreads moved with no macro trapdoor underneath, which makes it a positioning and risk-premium event. Bunds are the lifeboat, so look at the Bund/OAT/BTP relative trade and at banks with big domestic sovereign books.
items.tweetA: The Italy 2y spread nearly doubled to 55bp in one session and nobody called it a crisis because the number still looks small. That is how fragmentation starts: the front end reprices first, the 10y follows. Watch BTP-Bund 2y before you watch OATs.
items.tweetB: France didn't fall off a macro cliff. Goldman has growth at 0.1% for a month. What changed is the price someone wants to hold the tail. That's a risk-premium regime change, not a data surprise, and those don't mean-revert on a budget speech.

charts.desc: Goldman chart on OAT-Bund spread and French CDS inside the email; spread at 141bp vs 2012 peak is the tweetable image

items.title: Goldman's debt arithmetic: France needs a 1% primary surplus to stabilise debt, 2% at market rates, a level it has never recorded
items.idea: Goldman sees French debt rising toward 125% of GDP by the start of the next decade while the average interest rate climbs from ~2% to ~3%. Stabilising the ratio needs a primary surplus around 1% of GDP, something France rarely managed in 35 years. Mark the stock at current market rates and the hurdle rises toward 2%, which it has never posted. Melenchon's proposal to cancel Banque de France-held debt is called illegal by the BdF governor.
items.angle: The r-g math is what the bond market is pricing, not the Friday budget. The tail case (debt cancellation) is low probability but goes at the legal rulebook, so it prices into the term premium and CDS first.
items.tweetA: The French budget on Friday cuts the deficit to 5% from 5.4%. Goldman says to hold the debt ratio flat at today's market rates you'd need a primary surplus of ~2% of GDP, which France has never printed. 0.4 points of deficit cut is a rounding error against that.
items.tweetB: Low-probability, high-impact: a Melenchon win is a small tail in Goldman's simulation, yet his policy is cancelling debt held by the central bank. Bondholders don't need the probability to be high. They need the payoff to be asymmetric, and it is.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Barclays / Fidelity)
items.title: Euro bonds sold off while ECB hike pricing fell: Barclays calls it 'fragmentation' price action, and hedge funds capitulated on a French trade
items.idea: Swaps no longer fully price three more ECB hikes, down from at least four on Tuesday, yet most euro government bonds outside Germany and the Netherlands still sold off. Barclays' Khanna called the price action unusual and compared it with fragmentation periods. Fidelity's Mike Riddell says funds were long short-dated French bonds against swaps and Thursday looked like capitulation. US Treasury yields rose in the European session before reversing.
items.angle: When duration sells off alongside lower rate expectations you are in a term premium or credit event. The trade to watch is who still holds the short-dated French-vs-swaps position and whether the unwind has more to go.
items.tweetA: Normally lower hike odds means bonds rally. Euro govies sold off anyway. When the rate path and the bond price move in opposite directions, the market isn't pricing the ECB, it's pricing the sovereign. Different asset, different risk premium.
items.tweetB: Treasuries sold off in the European session, then reversed once Europe closed. Read that as the US long end being hostage to euro-area fiscal stress for a few hours. The global term premium is one market now, and Paris is a node in it.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Citadel Securities / Frank Flight)
items.title: Citadel's Frank Flight: Iran is long a high-strike oil call with a political expiry, and its Hormuz leverage is near peak gamma
items.idea: Flight frames Hormuz as optionality whose value depends on both the oil price and the political calendar (US midterms). Gamma is high but so is theta: the closer oil sits to the political pain threshold while the calendar runs down, the more valuable the leverage and the faster it decays. If Brent shows upside exhaustion, holding the position open pays less, which creates an incentive to monetise by reopening Hormuz in exchange for a broader settlement.
items.angle: A cleaner way to size the settlement-headline tail: if leverage is peaking before midterms, the asymmetry in crude is a sharp drop on a deal. Pair with the diesel and China export-ban data for what is not priced into products.
items.tweetA: Iran is long an oil call that expires at the US midterms. Peak gamma means the option is worth the most right now, and theta says it's about to start bleeding. Sellers of that option get paid in a settlement. The question for $CL is who is positioned for the exercise.
items.tweetB: Everyone is long the Hormuz risk premium. Almost nobody is asking what Tehran does when its own option starts decaying. Monetising leverage before expiry is the rational move, and a deal headline is a gap-down in crude, not a drift.

items.title: Diesel Danger Zone: NY Harbor ULSD near $230/bbl, US pump above $6.50/gal for the first time, and the term structure says chronic, not transitory
items.idea: Seaborne exports from the world's largest diesel exporters are down 1-1.5 mmbpd as the Hormuz crisis and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries remove supply. Futures hit all-time highs near $230/bbl in NY Harbor and US average pump prices topped $6.50/gal. Diesel can't be dark-transited or pipeline-rerouted: it needs refining capacity. China isn't exporting, Europe is sitting on reserves, and the US is weighing a diesel export ban ahead of midterms.
items.angle: Diesel is a tax on every supply chain, so the demand destruction will show up as margin compression and PMI prices paid. Refiners and tanker owners are the obvious longs; aggregates and freight are the margin victims.
items.tweetA: $230 ULSD, $6.50 at the pump, and the curve says it stays. Crude can be rerouted, SPR can be released. Diesel needs a refinery, and the world just lost a big chunk of them. The market is searching for a price that kills demand, and we haven't found it yet. $VLO $MPC
items.tweetB: A US diesel export ban is the single worst policy option on the table and also the most likely when pump prices hit $6.50 a month before an election. Ban exports and you hand the shortage to Europe and Latin America while US crack spreads blow out at home. Backfire guaranteed.

items.title: Oil resumes rally as China bans October fuel exports; US asks France and Germany to release diesel stocks
items.idea: Mando's macro roll lists: oil resumes rally as China bans October fuel exports; US asks France and Germany to release diesel stocks; Gulf oil exports doubled in September; US-asks-Iranian-delegation-to-leave (Rubio); UK cites strong indications of Iranian involvement in a bomb plot. SixSigma has crude near $90.98 at the open.
items.angle: This is the other half of the diesel story: China closing the tap and Washington asking Europe to open reserves. The Gulf export doubling in September cuts against pure supply-shock narrative; need to see where those barrels went.
items.tweetA: China banning October fuel exports while Washington begs Europe to release diesel. The two largest policy levers on products are pointing in opposite directions, and Gulf exports doubled in September. Something doesn't reconcile in the crude balance, and it's usually the products.
items.tweetB: If Beijing hoards fuel and Brussels hoards diesel, the marginal barrel gets priced by the US, and the US is thinking about banning exports. Three policy decisions, one price. $XLE

items.title: US 10y at its highest since 2002 (Mando) vs 2007 (Unchained), with a cool PCE and a 17-month-high dollar
items.idea: Mando: US PCE came in cool (partly due to a methodology change, savings rate at a 3-year low) yet yields still surged, with the 10y at its highest since 2002 and the dollar at a 17-month high. Goldman pushed its second Fed hike to December. Unchained's Laura Shin opens with the 10y at its highest 'since 2007' in the same session. Q2 GDP +2.2% q/q and ADP topped estimates.
items.angle: The two sources disagree on the lookback (2002 vs 2007), so check the print before quoting. Core point: a cool inflation print did not help the long end. Real yield and supply are the driver, not the Fed path.
items.tweetA: Cool PCE, savings rate at a 3-year low, and the 10y still goes to a multi-decade high. When the soft data can't rally the long end, you're not trading inflation expectations anymore. You're trading who owns the supply.
items.tweetB: The PCE 'beat' came with a methodology change. The savings rate is at a 3-year low. Consumers are funding spending out of buffer while the 10y reprices to a 2002 level. Something has to give, and it won't be yields.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Bloomberg's Simon White / Goldman's Privorotsky)
items.title: Treasuries look cheap against GDP, global yields and stocks, but White says they're not washed out yet
items.idea: Treasuries screen cheap vs nominal GDP, global yields and macro fair-value models, and increasingly competitive vs stocks given a compressed ERP. But White's historical-return framework says the downside overshoot that marks a durable turn isn't there. Most of the move is in real yields, not breakevens, and his leading indicators say pressure persists. Higher yields feed vol, thinner liquidity and tighter risk limits, and the deficit keeps term premium sticky.
items.angle: Valuation says start scaling; timing says wait. A good frame for a rules-based approach: buy cheap-vs-equity only after the real-yield momentum signal turns.
items.tweetA: Cheap is not the same as oversold. Treasuries now yield enough to compete with expensive equities, and still the buyers are not stepping in. The valuation case arrived before the timing case. That gap is where people get hurt.
items.tweetB: Real yields did the damage, not breakevens. That means inflation isn't the bear case for duration. The bear case is supply plus vol-targeting funds forced to sell when the numbers get big.

items.title: ISM manufacturing 54.5: new orders 55.3, backlogs 56.4, prices paid +7pts to 77.9, 16 of 18 industries paying more
items.idea: September ISM was 54.5 vs 54.6, new orders up 1.6 to 55.3 and backlogs up 4.6 to 56.4. Inventories fell to 48.6 and customer inventories sit at 41.6, very lean. Supplier deliveries at 59 show lengthening lead times, and prices paid jumped almost 7 points to 77.9, a four-month high. Sixteen of 18 industries reported paying more. The title also flags French and Italian bond yields at highs of day.
items.angle: An ISM at 54.5 with customer inventories at 41.6 is a restocking cycle with no cushion, and prices paid at 78 meets diesel above $6.50. That is the goods-side inflation channel that the PCE method change hid.
items.tweetA: Customer inventories at 41.6 with backlogs rising. That is the thinnest cushion you can have going into a restock. Add prices paid at 77.9 and you have a manufacturing recovery that runs straight into the diesel shock.
items.tweetB: ISM at 54.5, prices paid at 78, supplier deliveries at 59. That is a supply-constrained expansion. The Fed's problem is not weak demand, it's an economy that can't deliver what it's ordering.

items.title: Trump tells Powell to resign or face a lawsuit; Fed watchdog cleared him on the renovation probe; Goldman pushes second hike to December
items.idea: From the macro roll: Trump tells Powell to resign or face a lawsuit; the Fed IG cleared Powell in the renovation probe; Goldman delays its second Fed hike forecast to December; Treasury will buy back $6B of longer-term debt; foreigners dumped 3.6 trillion yen of Japan bonds in a week; German inflation at its highest since 2023; French 10y at a 24-year high.
items.angle: Fed independence, buyback support for the long end, and foreign selling of JGBs are three separate pressure points on the global term premium. The tail risk is a Fed-leadership headline hitting a market with no bid in the long end.
items.tweetA: A president threatening to sue the Fed chair, a Treasury buying back $6B of long bonds to defend the curve, and foreigners selling 3.6 trillion yen of JGBs in one week. Three signals that the long end has lost its marginal buyer. $TLT
items.tweetB: The inspector general cleared Powell and the White House responded by escalating. The renovation probe was never the point. The point is that with the 10y at multi-decade highs, a Fed-independence headline lands on a market with thin liquidity.

items.title: SPY rejects the 21 EMA and closes below the 50-day; 100-day at 754, 200-day at 720, jobs report tomorrow
items.idea: SPY gapped up into the underside of the 21 EMA, rejected and closed below the 50-day again. Rising rates keep pressuring everything. Next support is the 100-day at 754 (a 1% drop would lose it), then the 200-day at 720. He calls the structure still a bull flag, a fakeout before a rip is possible, but advises taking chips off if levered with the jobs report tomorrow.
items.angle: Useful levels: 754 and 720. The levered trader is the marginal seller if the 100-day goes. Cross-check against Bradstreet's note that he cut AI exposure to 34% of net.
items.tweetA: SPY rejected the 21 EMA and is under the 50-day. Next stops are 754 and 720. The market is going into a jobs print with rates at multi-decade highs and a dollar at a 17-month high. This isn't a setup for max risk.
items.tweetB: Rates up, dollar up, oil up, and SPY still holding a 'bull flag'. Either the flag resolves higher on a soft jobs number, or the 100-day goes and the levered crowd is forced out. Binary, with the print as the trigger.

items.title: September's S&P leaders: 13 of the top 20 were tech, Moderna +553% YTD, Intel and Bloom >200%, Dell +327%; FICO lost 48% in a month
items.idea: Tech was 13 of September's 20 best S&P 500 stocks. Everpure led with +40.7%, then Moderna, Intel and Bloom Energy each above +30%. Moderna is +553% YTD, Intel and Bloom more than +200%, Dell +327.35%. Meta +26.7% in September is just +9.86% YTD. On the loser side, FICO fell 48.36% and Gen Digital 28.97%, with tech also holding the two worst names; ten of eleven sectors appear in the bottom 20 and 18 of the 20 laggards are down YTD.
items.angle: A month where the worst stock fell nearly 20 points more than the second-worst is a dispersion regime. Memory, power, and Intel all in the winners list ties to the Micron print. FICO -48% is the AI-disruption-of-incumbents trade.
items.tweetA: Moderna up 553% YTD sits on the same winners list as Intel and Dell. This is not a quality rally, it's a momentum and beta rally. And the same month FICO lost half its value. Dispersion is the regime, and the index is hiding it.
items.tweetB: Bloom +200% YTD, Dell +327%, Intel +200%. The AI trade moved from 'buy the chips' to 'buy anything that touches power and servers'. When the second derivative is the leader, it's late, not wrong.

items.title: September was a historic month of equal-weight (RSP) underperformance versus cap-weight (SPY)
items.idea: Bespoke says September was a historic month of underperformance for the S&P 500 equal-weight index vs the cap-weighted index. Nikkei +3% and Kospi nearly +2% on Micron's earnings 'triple play'; STOXX 600 -0.6% with little tech exposure to benefit, so oil and yields dominated. Manufacturing PMIs beat in Europe and accelerated in Japan and South Korea.
items.angle: Breadth: RSP down more than 4% and IWM down 4.16% in August (Bradstreet), then a record gap in September. Concentration risk is at a record just as the long end breaks.
items.tweetA: Equal-weight lost to cap-weight by a record margin in September while the 10y printed a multi-decade high. The index is holding up because of a handful of names that are the least rate-sensitive. That is not breadth, it's concentration.
items.tweetB: Europe is down 0.6% because it owns almost nothing that Micron helps. Asia is up 3% because it owns all of it. The single best macro hedge against rates this month was owning memory.

items.title: A fund up 77.58% YTD cuts AI exposure to 34% of net but calls it 'the highest EV spot' and the tail risk 'blown out'
items.idea: Bradstreet's L/S account is +97.36% and L/O +53.42%, +77.58% blended YTD (65.82% at end of August). He cut AI-trade exposure to 34% of net, raised healthcare to 37.43%, and describes 'sticking the landing': reduce exposure modestly in the most efficient way while still making high-EV plays. SMH +12% in September while RSP fell over 4% and IWM 4.16% in August.
items.angle: A practitioner telling you he trims because tails are widening while still calling it the best EV in the market is the honest version of where many funds sit.
items.tweetA: +77% YTD and he's cut AI to 34% of net. Not because the thesis broke, but because the tail got blown out. That's what late-cycle discipline looks like: stay long the best EV, shrink the size. Compare that with how most funds are positioned.
items.tweetB: Healthcare 37.43% of net, AI 34%. Two sleeves that together are most of the book. The portfolio is a barbell between the AI compute trade and the biotech tail. Neither correlates with the rate shock, which is the point.

items.title: Aggregates thesis: 3 respected 13F filers are long CRH/VMC/MLM; rock is 1-5% of project cost, so diesel gets passed through
items.idea: Bradstreet entered CRH, VMC and MLM after seeing Duquesne long CRH, TCI (Chris Hohn) long VMC and MLM, and Voss long TTAM, entering below their cost basis. Diesel hits the group (excavators, trucks, crushers) but aggregates are 1-5% of project cost, supply is local because freight prices out competitors, and producers just want gross profit per tonne to grow faster than inflation. He contrasts it with an 80% DRAM price rise inside a data center budget. Demand is data centers, LNG plants, fabs and infrastructure despite the weakest single-family housing.
items.angle: A pass-through-pricing trade against the diesel spike in the energy items today. The bear case he names: nothing outside semis works until the singularity.
items.tweetA: Aggregates are 1-5% of a project's cost and the quarry can't be moved. A data center buyer paying 80% more for DRAM won't blink at 15% more for gravel. That's pricing power the market is discounting because diesel is spiking. $VMC $MLM
items.tweetB: Vulcan trades like an inflation bond, says one PM. Rock is heavy, cheap, and local, so freight is the moat. When diesel hits $230 the same diesel that squeezes margins also protects every regional quarry from outside competition.

items.title: Three 13F filers he respects (Duquesne, TCI, Voss) converge on aggregates and cement, and he buys below their cost basis
items.idea: He doesn't rate many 13F filers but three he does are in the same sector at the same time, and his entry prices are below theirs. Combined with bio sleeve wins (Biodesix price target $38 per HC Wainwright, Exagen under 3x sales with 20% growth, Quanterix 2.42 to 3.71), the note is a window into an idiosyncratic book.
items.angle: 13F convergence is a signal only if the filers have independent processes. Check for overlapping holders in the cement names.
items.tweetA: When three funds that don't coordinate all buy the same unglamorous sector, the interesting question isn't what they see. It's what the crowd sees that makes them comfortable buying below consensus entry.
items.tweetB: Quanterix went from $2.42 to $3.71 in under two months on a business nobody was watching. The mean-reversion trade on distressed small cap tools is the quietest alpha in a market obsessed with semis.

items.title: VEON announces a 3.9% buyback worth ~$200M: 27.5% of trailing equity FCF and a 5.5% yield, in a Pakistan/Ukraine/Kazakhstan oil-sensitive footprint
items.idea: VEON's Sept 23 program covers 72.5M shares (~$200M at $69.37/ADS), equal to 27.5% of TTM equity FCF after leases and licenses and a 5.5% yield on the trailing average price. Shares will be cancelled. Bradstreet trimmed 10% of a long-held position on the thesis that Pakistan and Bangladesh get buried by oil and Ukraine has a tough winter, and was punished. Kazakhstan benefits from high oil, giving a partial hedge.
items.angle: A frontier telco with FCF returned at a high rate, and a PM admitting he sold too early on a macro call. Good lesson on macro-driven trims.
items.tweetA: VEON is buying back 27.5% of trailing free cash flow. That's a company telling you what it thinks of its own stock in a market where oil is hurting two of its biggest countries. $VEON
items.tweetB: The trade nobody talks about: a frontier telco in Pakistan, Ukraine and Kazakhstan with a 5.5% buyback yield. High oil hurts two markets and helps one. It's the cheapest way to own an AI-efficiency story outside the US.

items.title: El Pollo Loco at 12x earnings: SNAP-heavy California customers make it 'recession proof', a 6.5% position
items.idea: Bradstreet bought LOCO at a P/E of 12 after a turnaround that expanded margins; growth stalled last quarter and the stock backed off from $17, but same-store sales stayed positive. He argues downside is limited because the chain sells food cheaply and many California customers pay with SNAP; the position is 6.5% of NAV. Also notes Nintendo was sized up as a hedge for a large memory position and is now down slightly.
items.angle: SNAP exposure as a consumer-health signal. Midterm-year Medicaid and SNAP policy matters for low-income QSR traffic.
items.tweetA: A PM sizing a QSR at 6.5% because its customers pay with SNAP. That's a curious definition of 'recession proof': it works until SNAP policy changes. Legal immigrants losing Medicaid is in today's headlines. $LOCO
items.tweetB: At a P/E of 12 with positive same-store sales, LOCO is priced for a recession that its own customers can't afford to start. The market assumes cheap food is defensive. It's only defensive if the subsidy stays.

items.title: The 'revenue meta': sort DeFiLlama by 30-day revenue, then ask three questions before buying the token
items.idea: With BTC above the $83k level, the altcoins that outperformed (HYPE, LIT, ENA, UNI) are tied to revenue. His framework: start with the DeFiLlama revenue dashboard, add TVL, price and revenue to the protocol chart, then ask whether revenue is rising, whether holders directly benefit, and whether there's a catalyst. Aave (28th by 30d revenue) fails on buybacks (paused since the April rsETH exploit) but passes on catalysts; Morpho is growing faster than Aave but has no value accrual so he prefers AAVE.
items.angle: Revenue is only valuation-relevant if holders capture it. A clean screen for the next rotation, and the Morpho vs Aave contrast shows 'growth without accrual' as the trap.
items.tweetA: Morpho is growing faster than Aave and he'd still rather own AAVE, because Morpho's token captures nothing. In a revenue meta, accrual beats growth. Most of the alt market hasn't priced that difference.
items.tweetB: Aave's buyback has been paused since April and it still screens as a buy. A restart is the catalyst that's priced as a maybe. Tokens with an announced-but-unscheduled buyback are the cheapest optionality in the revenue meta.

items.title: CHAD: a Solana-treasury perpetual preferred at a 13% variable dividend, issued only when it trades at $10+
items.idea: DFDV sells CHAD at $8, $10 stated value, 13% annual variable dividend, issuing new shares only when it trades above $10 to buy more SOL. Treasury holds 2.5M SOL, up ~10% in six weeks. It is explicitly modelled on Strategy's STRC, which the author notes fell during the BTC crash. Flagged as sponsored.
items.angle: Sponsored content, but the structure is the point: perps issued at a premium to fund coin accumulation are reflexive and fail when the underlying drops.
items.tweetA: 13% variable dividend, issued only above $10, funding more SOL. The flywheel works while the coin goes up. STRC already showed what happens in a BTC crash. A perpetual preferred is only senior if the common holds its value.
items.tweetB: 2.5M SOL, a 13% preferred and a stock that follows the coin. That's a levered SOL ETF with a credit spread attached. The real question is what the dividend is paid from when SOL doesn't go up.

items.title: SEC gives the green light for token buybacks; Hyperliquid team sells $320M of HYPE OTC to an 'institution'

items.angle: Buyback legality is what turns 'revenue meta' into a legal cash-flow narrative. A $320M HYPE sale into strength is the supply overhang for the leading revenue token.
items.tweetA: The SEC just made token buybacks legal. The team behind the biggest revenue token is selling $320M of it at the same time. Both can be true: buybacks make the asset a cash-flow instrument, and insiders know it.
items.tweetB: Ethena ends USDe incentives, the SEC greenlights buybacks, Aave lends against tokenized Coinbase stock. The 2021 DeFi playbook of emissions is being swapped for the TradFi playbook of buybacks and collateral. That's the regime change.

items.title: Bitget hacked for ~$352M, Trezor breach a few weeks ago: the 'self-custody' meme is losing its bite
items.idea: Bitget lost roughly $352M this week; withdrawals are back. A few weeks earlier Trezor warned 14,000 users after a fulfilment partner data breach. Mando adds hackers moved 2.7K ZEC into a pool, MetaMask had a security incident on infrastructure, and Bitget plans to resume all withdrawals.
items.angle: Custody risk is the credit risk of crypto. The exchange-hack-to-recovery cycle that's now routine is what keeps institutional allocators on regulated custody.
items.tweetA: Bitget loses $352M and withdrawals resume within days. That's not a hack, that's a balance sheet event with a reserve fund behind it. The tail isn't the hack, it's the exchange that can't pay out.
items.tweetB: Exchange hack, hardware wallet breach, MetaMask infra incident, all in a month. 'Not your keys' has been the answer for a decade. The new answer is that your keys leak through the supply chain.

items.title: Hester Peirce leaves the SEC Oct 2; CFTC clears tokenized collateral; Senate Republicans introduce a crypto tax bill; Illinois drafts a profit-or-loss tax
items.idea: Hester Peirce, the SEC's 'Crypto Mom', leaves on October 2. CFTC finally allows futures brokers to use tokenized assets as collateral, and sent the White House new prediction-market rules. Senate Republicans introduced a crypto tax bill; Illinois drafted a mark-to-market 'profit or loss' tax. The UK started licensing, the EU is scrutinising Binance's MiCA exemption, Korea proposed tokenization rules.
items.angle: The champion at the SEC leaves just as buybacks and exemptions are being written. Who replaces her matters more than the individual rules.
items.tweetA: Peirce leaves the SEC tomorrow. The innovation exemption and the buyback guidance were written under her watch. The rules are in place. The question is whether the next commissioner enforces the spirit or the letter.
items.tweetB: A federal crypto tax bill, an Illinois mark-to-market tax, UK licensing and MiCA scrutiny on Binance, all in one week. Regulation isn't a binary anymore. It's 50 jurisdictions each writing a slightly different rulebook.

items.title: Encrypted conditional orders: Nillion Covenants let you pre-commit 'short TSM if a 6.5 quake hits Taiwan' without anyone seeing the trigger or size
items.idea: Onchain trading is 'poker with cards face-up': positions, strategy and timing are visible to front-runners. Blocmates says AI can doxx you for under $2 in under a minute. Nillion's Covenants are encrypted if-then instructions sealed until a condition fires, e.g. 'short TSM if a 6.5 quake hits Taiwan' or 'max short BTC if any of Satoshi's coins move'. Also sealed-bid token sales.
items.angle: Privacy is the missing primitive for institutional onchain execution. A quake-triggered TSM short is the kind of hedge a desk would want automated and hidden.
items.tweetA: Short $TSM if a 6.5 quake hits Taiwan, sealed until the trigger. If this works you can pre-commit hedges against geopolitical tails without telegraphing the book. That's a new primitive for macro funds, not a DeFi toy.
items.tweetB: AI can doxx you for under $2 in a minute. Meanwhile onchain, your whole book is public. The privacy trade isn't ideological anymore. It's execution quality.

items.title: Quant (QNT) went from $67 to $288 in nine days on a Clearing House pick; the Quant founder moved $7M of QNT after 7 years
items.idea: Blocmates reports the Clearing House's Quant pick sent QNT from $67 to $288 in nine days (4.3x). Mando notes the Quant founder moved $7M of QNT after 7 years. Separately Zama's shielded TVL went from $85M to $90M in four days.
items.angle: An institutional-infrastructure name catching a narrative bid and a founder wallet moving at the same time is the classic distribution pattern.
items.tweetA: QNT 4.3x in nine days on an institutional-plumbing narrative, then the founder moves $7M after seven years of silence. Doesn't prove anything. But when both happen in the same week, the wallet is the more honest signal.
items.tweetB: Clearing-house infrastructure goes 4.3x in nine days. This is what the 'tokenization is the product-market fit' thesis looks like when it's priced by retail. The plumbing trade is crowded.

items.title: Neuner: Bessent doubling Treasury buybacks started the crypto bull market, and he may be 'engineering the ultimate short squeeze'
items.idea: Neuner argues the crypto bull began when Bessent took on the bond market and said he'd double buybacks, but $4-6B buybacks are 'fists into a big fight' against long yields. Yesterday's hot PMI and a struggling 5-year auction scared the bond market; with ~$1T in the TGA the Treasury could buy far more. He thinks Bessent is waiting for bond vigilantes to short the long end, then squeeze them by injecting liquidity.
items.angle: A bullish-liquidity thesis at multi-decade-high yields. The test is the size of the next buyback, which was $6B today.
items.tweetA: $6B of buybacks against a 10y at multi-decade highs and a TGA with $1T in it. If Bessent is engineering a squeeze he's showing the small hand first. The scenario depends on the size of the next buyback, not the first.
items.tweetB: Crypto bulls are now underwriting a Treasury put at the long end. That's a macro thesis with one catalyst and a TGA balance as the sole evidence. If Treasury doesn't scale up, the thesis is just hope with a chart.

charts.desc: Neuner's ETH/BTC 9-year downtrend breakout chart and AI-vs-crypto NASDAQ chart (on screen in the video)

items.title: ETH/BTC breaks a 9-year downtrend; 'crypto's first bull market' rests on tokenization and a billion AI agents doing 217B transactions a day
items.idea: Neuner shows ETH/BTC breaking a 9-year downtrend, which he reads as the first use case besides Bitcoin's store-of-value to create sustained outperformance: tokenization. He then cites a BlackRock report saying agentic AI and machine-to-machine payments will raise demand for blockchains and stablecoins, and a study of 1 billion agents by 2029 executing 217 billion transactions a day. The thread of the episode: crypto is infrastructure for agents.
items.angle: The 217B-transaction figure is the thing to stress-test. A transaction count isn't a fee pool, and agent payments may go to the cheapest rail, not the most decentralized.
items.tweetA: 217 billion agent transactions a day by 2029. Divide any fee pool by that number and see what each transaction can afford to pay. Agent payments go to the cheapest rail, and that is rarely the one with the best token.
items.tweetB: BlackRock says agent payments favor programmable rails over ACH and cards. That's a TradFi sponsor writing the bull case for stablecoins. If ETH/BTC has really broken a 9-year trend, this is the narrative that sustains it.

items.title: Crypto flows: BTC ETF streak ends (-$149M), crypto products +$3.55B last week, BTC and ETH post highest monthly closes of 2026
items.idea: BTC $83,662, ETH $2,687, SOL $117; fear and greed at 73; 24h liquidations $289M. Bitcoin ETFs -$149M, ETH ETFs -$60M, ending the BTC inflow streak. Crypto products saw $3.55B inflows last week; short-term BTC holders sit on ~13% profit; Hayes outlines a path to $1M BTC by 2030; Schwab says a strong USD and oil won't crush BTC. Adler's note says BTC has held above short-term holders' average cost for several weeks.
items.angle: Highest monthly close of 2026 plus ETF outflows plus fear and greed at 73: a late-run market with a thin buffer vs rates.
items.tweetA: Highest monthly close of 2026 for both BTC and ETH, and the ETF inflow streak ends the same day. Short-term holders are 13% in profit. That's a market with a cushion, but it's the type of cushion that gets tested by a 10y breakout.
items.tweetB: Crypto products took in $3.55B last week and BTC ETFs just saw outflows. Flows led price on the way up. Watch whether they lead on the way down.

items.title: Korea trades $3.8B a day in crypto across 11.13M accounts but has tokenized only $450M of RWAs
items.idea: Korea had 11.13M eligible crypto accounts (over 20% of the population) at end-2025 and ~5.4 trillion won (~$3.8B) of daily volume, but only ~640 billion won (~$450M) in tokenized RWAs, mostly music royalties (65%) and art (17%). Global tokenized assets are about $37.3B. The KSD September guideline limits token securities to private ledgers from February 2027; the Digital Asset Basic Act may require banks to hold 50%+1 of any KRW stablecoin issuer. Report disclosed as partly funded by Monad.
items.angle: Sponsored research, but the numbers show a retail-heavy market with the regulatory plumbing still unbuilt. The KRW stablecoin issuer rule (bank majority) is the key tell.
items.tweetA: Korea trades $3.8B a day and has tokenized $450M. Daily volume is 8x the entire stock of RWAs. This is a casino with a country-sized user base waiting for a legal rail to become a financial system.
items.tweetB: If the Digital Asset Basic Act forces banks to own 50%+1 of any KRW stablecoin issuer, a Stripe-style neutral issuer gets pushed to infrastructure. Korea may build the first bank-controlled stablecoin regime in a major economy.

items.title: The SWIFT study: adopting the network raised bank profitability ~40% over ten years, 6x more for small banks
items.idea: Scott, Van Reenen and Zachariadis (2017), 6,848 banks in 29 countries: adopting SWIFT raised profitability around 40% over the next decade, small and starting slowly. For small banks the effect was ~6x larger than for big ones, attributed to access to counterparties they couldn't reach before. Tiger uses this to argue shared on-chain infrastructure could help Korean regional banks. Other items: Korea's WGBI inclusion could bring 70-90 trillion won of passive inflows and the BoK's offshore won network opens January 2027.
items.angle: A useful analogue for settlement-layer adoption: benefits go to the long tail of institutions. Treat the Monad pitch as marketing but the SWIFT paper as real.
items.tweetA: SWIFT adoption raised bank profitability ~40% over a decade, and small banks gained 6x more than big ones. Settlement networks are a democratizing technology for the long tail. That's the best argument for stablecoin rails I've seen, and it has nothing to do with crypto.
items.tweetB: WGBI inclusion should bring 70-90 trillion won in passive inflows to Korean bonds. The offshore won network opens in January. Korea is building the pipes for global capital to hold won, and the tokenization story is a layer on top.

items.title: Micron FQ4: $54.23B revenue (+31% q/q, ~5x y/y), non-GAAP EPS $33.42, 87% gross margin
items.idea: SixSigma's open note: Micron reported fiscal Q4 2026 revenue of $54.23B, up 31% sequentially and roughly 5x year-over-year, non-GAAP EPS of $33.42 and an 87% gross margin. Bespoke calls it an earnings 'triple play' that lifted Nikkei (+3%) and Kospi (nearly +2%). Mando: Micron says humanoids may need 200GB+ of DRAM. Bradstreet notes an 80% DRAM price rise as a budget item inside data centers.
items.angle: An 87% gross margin on memory is not a commodity margin. It's a rationed-supply margin. The risk is a DRAM capex response in 2027.
items.tweetA: 87% gross margin on DRAM. That's not a cyclical peak, that's a scarcity price. Revenue 5x in a year means customers are paying whatever it takes to get bits. The only thing that breaks this is supply, and the supply response takes 18 months. $MU
items.tweetB: Micron quarterly revenue of $54B is bigger than most S&P 500 companies' annual sales, and a year ago it was a fifth of that. The AI trade now has a sustained-scarcity thesis, not a demand one. Humanoids needing 200GB+ of DRAM each is the next leg.

items.title: Amazon signs a 20-year, 690MW nuclear PPA with Constellation; CoreWeave puts Vera Rubin NVL72 into production with 4.8x token throughput
items.idea: AMZN signed a 20-year PPA with Constellation for 690MW from Calvert Cliffs, unlocking $3B including 190MW of new capacity between 2030 and 2032; AWS signed a >$1B multi-year chip-design licensing deal with Synopsys for Trainium and Graviton. CoreWeave put NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems into production, with Cognition first on production workloads and up to 4.8x higher token throughput. Also LLY's oral obesity drug Foundayo cut the risk of type 2 diabetes 57% and RKLB won a 20-launch Electron contract.
items.angle: Power is bought in 20-year increments while chips turn over every 12 months. That mismatch is the structural risk for the grid-capacity trade.
items.tweetA: 20-year nuclear PPA for a chip cycle that turns over every year. Amazon is locking the one input that can't be reordered. Of everything in AI infra, power is the only line item where the supply response is measured in decades. $CEG $AMZN
items.tweetB: 4.8x higher token throughput on Vera Rubin. If one generation of hardware delivers that, the cost per token halves faster than demand doubles. That's the only way the $6T AI revenue number gets less scary.

items.title: Anthropic's IPO filing shows Broadcom may lend up to $42B via convertibles to help finance a $125.2B, five-year TPU lease
items.idea: TWiST's top stories: Anthropic's IPO filing shows Broadcom may lend up to $42B through convertible notes, potentially financing a five-year $125.2B TPU lease and deepening dependence on strategic infrastructure partners (Reuters). Also Salesforce acquiring Listen Labs for a reported $2B, ElevenLabs doubling its valuation to $22B via a $300M employee tender, and Armadin's $255.5M Series B at a $2.5B valuation.
items.angle: Vendor financing for a compute lease is the circular-financing pattern from past capex booms, now at $125B scale. Cross-check with Blocmates' $6T-of-revenue-by-2031 claim.
items.tweetA: A chip vendor lending up to $42B to its customer so the customer can lease $125B of the vendor's chips. Call it what it is: vendor financing. We've seen the movie, and the sequel has a bigger budget. $AVGO
items.tweetB: $125.2B over five years is $25B a year of TPU rent. A lease that size means the IPO is funding a commitment, not just growth.

items.title: Google's Gemini 4 Argon: 1M-token output, priced well below rivals, limited to 'trusted cyber defenders', reportedly weak on coding
items.idea: Google began rolling out Gemini 4 Argon. Mando adds: 1M-token output window, priced well below rivals (The Information), access limited to 'trusted cyber defenders' (The Verge), and reportedly struggles on coding. Meta's Muse AI hit 5M downloads; DeepSeek open-sourced tools for Huawei AI chips; OpenAI flagged an alleged Chinese push to copy models (Moonshot's Kimi).
items.angle: Restricting a flagship to cyber defenders is the new release pattern for dual-use capability. Pricing below rivals is the margin attack.
items.tweetA: Google prices Argon well below rivals, limits it to trusted cyber defenders, and reports say it struggles on coding. A flagship you can't fully use, cheaply. Strategy is the product here, not the model.
items.tweetB: 1M-token output at below-rival pricing. If that holds, the competition moves from capability to cost per useful token. DeepSeek porting tools to Huawei chips puts a floor under that price on the other side.

items.title: FTC opens a 'rogue AI' probe of OpenAI, Anthropic and other labs over product harms
items.idea: TWiST and Mando both lead with the FTC investigation of OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies over potential product harms; zerohedge frames it as aimed at their 'regulatory moat'. Also: California's Newsom signed a ban on AI 'robo bosses', Trump's AI lunch included all big tech except Apple, and a report says AI could displace 11 million US workers by 2035.
items.angle: Regulatory risk now arrives with an IPO filing on the table for Anthropic. That's the timing to watch.
items.tweetA: FTC opens a probe of the labs the same week one of them has an IPO filing circulating. An investigation that lands in the S-1 risk section is a very different animal from one that lands in a press release.
items.tweetB: California bans AI 'robo bosses', the FTC opens a harms probe, Democrats can't agree on an AI platform. AI regulation in the US is going to be written by 50 states and one agency, none of which agree.

items.title: Security: hackers stole millions of US military personnel records; AI agents probed Canadian government networks; Pentagon taps Elon for Project Meridian
items.idea: Under AI & Tech: hackers stole millions of US military personnel records in a months-long breach (TechCrunch); AI agents targeted Canadian government networks in rudimentary attempts (Gizmodo); Pentagon taps Elon for 'Project Meridian'; Blue Origin's first external round was oversubscribed; McDonald's uses AI to price burgers.
items.angle: Cybersecurity plus defense plus AI are converging, and the AI Snake Oil piece argues cyber tail risk is the underpriced systemic risk.
items.tweetA: Millions of military personnel records stolen over months, AI agents probing Canada's networks, and the Pentagon handing Elon a project called Meridian. The attack surface and the procurement list are the same list.
items.tweetB: McDonald's is using AI to price a burger. Rudimentary AI hacks are hitting Canadian government networks. Same technology, one gets headlines, the other changes your margins.

items.title: DHH: 37signals is 'done writing code by hand' and the price of repetition has gone to near zero
items.idea: DHH told Rails World that writing code by hand at 37signals is now 'an exceptional state', like seeing a bug in Sentry, calling Opus 4.5 on Nov 24, 2025 the 'Kodak Brownie of our era'. The company is moving backends to Rust and building native apps with small teams, and he says abstractions make less sense when repetition costs almost nothing. He says he 'retired from being a professional programmer' around March. Also: at OpenAI non-engineering teams (finance, recruiting, legal) moved to Codex in June.
items.angle: The abstraction claim is the structural one: if repetition is free, architecture changes. That's the part to track in software cost curves.
items.tweetA: 'The price of repetition has gone to near zero.' That one sentence breaks a 50-year software principle. DRY existed because humans paid for duplicate code. Agents don't. Expect codebases to get bigger, uglier, and cheaper.
items.tweetB: The creator of Rails is moving backends to Rust because agents write 'good enough' Rust. Language choice used to be about developer productivity. Now it's about runtime cost, because the dev is free. $GTLB $MSFT

items.title: An anonymous Big Tech engineer: 'People are working 12 to 13 hours a day just to press enter. Nobody is reading anything.'
items.idea: A post by user voxium describes a big company where specs, code, tests, PRDs and tickets are all made by Claude Code, managers say pushing code is not the bottleneck, and nobody is reading output. Gergely says software quality has degraded since the start of the year, citing Spotify outages and an Uber Eats add-ons selector shipped with three visible bugs, including 'Choose up to 999'. He still argues software engineering becomes more important, with new work in validating agent output and replacing LLM calls with LLM-generated deterministic code.
items.angle: Quality decline from outsourced thinking is a measurable externality; the investable angle is the QA and validation layer.
items.tweetA: 'Choose up to 999' shipped to every Uber Eats user. Nobody on the team tested an empty field. When the agent writes the code and the agent writes the test, you have a system that agrees with itself. The market for independent verification is wide open.
items.tweetB: 12 to 13 hour days to press enter, shipping mandates, nobody reading. This isn't an AI productivity story. It's a throughput-at-all-costs story where quality is the shock absorber, and the bill comes later.

items.title: Vercel's AI gateway: 60% of model spend goes to open-weight models; OpenAI becomes a platform with 16 partners
items.idea: This week's Pulse (previewed in the footer): Vercel's AI gateway shows 60% of model spend going to open-weight models and OpenRouter shows open models being used more than closed ones. OpenAI is becoming a platform where ChatGPT spend can be allocated to open models and offerings from 16 partners. Also a Firebase iOS SDK outage that crashed apps for 2-6 hours, and why CTOs and VPEs are quitting en masse.
items.angle: If 60% of gateway spend is open-weight, the closed-model premium is narrower than headline revenue suggests. The OpenAI-as-AWS move is a defensive response.
items.tweetA: 60% of model spend on Vercel's gateway goes to open-weight models. Closed-model revenue is the headline, but the marginal dollar of developer spend is already open. OpenAI turning ChatGPT into a platform with 16 partners reads as an admission.
items.tweetB: A Firebase SDK change took down every app with Firebase analytics for 2-6 hours, and Google didn't post a postmortem. The single biggest AI risk isn't alignment, it's one SDK pushed on a Tuesday.

items.title: Millennium rolls out 150+ AI 'twins' with 97% daily usage; Citadel hiring AI-lab researchers; Heron AI-interviews ex-executives after earnings
items.idea: Millennium built a digital twin for its CIO and scaled to 150+ twins, with 97% of the first group interacting daily; twins have their own identity, email and audit trail, and AI 'teammates' are next. Citadel plans to grow its 180-person Global Quantitative Strategies team at a double-digit rate and recruit from labs like DeepMind. Heron interviews former executives within hours of earnings using AI.
items.angle: Quant shops and AI labs now compete for the same talent. A twin with its own permissions is the template for agent identity in finance.
items.tweetA: Millennium's AI twins have their own email, permissions and audit trail. That's not a chatbot, it's an employee with a compliance file. 97% daily usage in the first cohort says the adoption curve isn't the constraint.
items.tweetB: Citadel is hiring from DeepMind while Millennium clones its CIO. The edge in quant is shifting from data to who owns the best agents. The firms will start to look alike, and alpha decay speeds up.

items.title: Robinhood: 150,000 agent accounts in four months vs 28.6M funded customers, ~30M tool calls a day; the SEC cut footnote content by ~95% for AI readability
items.idea: Robinhood said 150,000+ customers signed up for an agent account in ~4 months, against 28.6M funded customers at end-August (about 0.5%), with agents using its tools almost 30 million times a day. Trade approvals are on by default for built-in agents. Webull's CEO notes the regulatory distinction between an agent following an instruction and one making an investment decision. The SEC is restructuring rule releases with tables and bullets and cut substantive footnote discussion 'something like 95%' so AI tools can read them.
items.angle: 30M tool calls a day from 150k accounts is ~200 calls per account per day. That's agent load, not human load. Brokerage infra is being re-sized for machines.
items.tweetA: 150,000 agent accounts, 30 million tool calls a day. That's 200 calls per account per day. A human doesn't do that. The retail broker's API is already an agent API, and the SEC is rewriting its rules for the same reader.
items.tweetB: The SEC cut footnote content by 95% so models can read its rules. The regulator is now writing for AI first and humans second. Compliance moves from lawyers reading to agents parsing.

items.title: AI-focused super PACs have spent ~$58M this cycle: $33M pro-safety vs $25M pro-innovation; Alex Bores lost his primary
items.idea: Democrats want to lead on AI but split into four camps (existential risk, AI-as-marketing, societal effects, environment). Transformer's tracker shows ~$58M by AI outside groups: $33M pro-safety and $25M pro-innovation. Alex Bores ran on strong AI regulation in NY-12 and lost after millions of outside spending. Sanders and Casar introduced a bill to ban superintelligent AI; Mamdani's NYC bans generative AI in school through 8th grade; Anthropic gave $40M to Public First Action. Over half of Gen Z uses gen AI but under 20% are optimistic.
items.angle: The pro-safety side is outspending pro-innovation, which is the opposite of the lobbying story many investors assume. 'AI midterms' means data centers become a candidate-level issue.
items.tweetA: Pro-safety super PACs have outspent pro-innovation $33M to $25M. The standard story is that Big Tech buys the regulators. This cycle the safety side has more money, and Anthropic wrote a $40M check to one of them.
items.tweetB: More than half of Gen Z uses generative AI and fewer than 1 in 5 is optimistic about it. Adoption without approval is a political time bomb. Data centers are the easy target, and they're exactly where the capex goes.

items.title: Trump's UNGA speech rebrands AI as 'super intelligence' (SI), conflating terms the industry already uses
items.idea: At the UN last week Trump said he would call 'artificial intelligence' 'super intelligence' or SI, in the wake of Dario Amodei's 'Pacing the Frontier' essay (co-signed by other frontier CEOs). The author argues the rebrand confuses terms already in use, may stoke the panic already underway and could harm the labs. Blocmates adds Trump told AI companies to 'police yourselves' while signing an SI accord, and that a 10-person committee will name a 'Super Intelligence Czar'.
items.angle: Words move policy: calling it SI reframes every regulatory conversation from products to existential capability. Check how it lands with the FTC probe.
items.tweetA: Trump says AI is now SI. Superintelligence is the term safety people use for the thing they want to ban. A president adopting it as branding is a gift to the Sanders-Casar bill. Rebrands have consequences.
items.tweetB: 'Police yourselves,' says the White House, while it signs an SI accord and builds a 10-person committee. The signal to labs is self-regulation. The signal to voters is that the president thinks this is SI-level. Those can't both be the policy.

items.title: Third possibility on x-risk: the warnings are sincere but wrong, and the doom framing pushes policy toward a ban instead of 100 resilience measures
items.idea: The authors argue the Coxon resignation made x-risk break through while the summer's agent-swarm hacks didn't. Gallup shows ~0.5% of Americans rate AI the most important issue: high concern, low salience. A 2019 WHO/World Bank report priced pandemic preparedness at $1-2 per person per year and most recommendations were never implemented. Lloyd's doesn't insure severe state-backed cyberattacks. Their 'big-tent' safety agenda: transparency and liability, resilience against catastrophic but sub-existential risks, and banning fully autonomous recursive self-improvement only after convincing skeptics.
items.angle: The cyber tail is the one with a credible causal path and no insurance. The investable angle is cyber resilience and liability regimes, not alignment.
items.tweetA: $1-2 per person per year would have bought pandemic preparedness. We didn't spend it. Lloyd's won't insure state-backed cyber attacks. The AI safety debate is arguing about extinction while the uninsurable risks we can model sit unfunded.
items.tweetB: A president, a Senate bill and 58M in super PAC money all aim at the same ban, because x-risk admits exactly one policy. Resilience needs 100 boring interventions. Politics can only sell the one with a villain.

items.title: How a few hundred conquistadors toppled two empires: outnumbered 100-1000x, with 99% of their forces drawn from the natives
items.idea: Dwarkesh frames the Aztec (6M people) and Inca (10M) conquests as among the most shocking events in history: Cortes took the Aztecs in about 2.5 years; Pizarro did the Inca a decade later. Conquistadors beat native armies while 100x or even 1000x outnumbered, sometimes without casualties, and 99% of their forces were the very natives they were subjugating. His thesis: 'AI takeover' is less unprecedented than it sounds, as an alien force using better technology and diplomacy can outmaneuver a larger existing order. Chapters include why Mughal India couldn't play Europeans off each other, and why diplomacy mattered as much as technology.
items.angle: The analogy for alliances and coalition politics: the leverage was local allies, not guns. Useful frame for tech-adoption and sovereign-alignment questions.
items.tweetA: 99% of Cortes's army were natives. The conquest wasn't a technology story, it was a coalition story. If you want to model how an outsider captures a larger system, look at who he persuaded, not what he carried.
items.tweetB: 100x outnumbered and winning, because the defenders were fighting each other. Same pattern in every platform war. The incumbent's real threat is never the newcomer's tech. It's the incumbent's own enemies who sign up with the newcomer.

items.title: Junior-mining owner-operator Gentile on what could break his gold thesis; Bastion manages C$700M+ and is top holder in 25+ juniors
items.idea: Sinn interviews Michael Gentile (Bastion Asset Management, over C$700M, reportedly the largest shareholder in more than 25 junior miners by early 2026). The conversation covers what could go wrong for a bullish gold and junior-mining thesis, political developments supportive of Canadian mining, and portfolio names (Valkea, Galway, Canex, Cascadia, Maple Gold). The email contains only the intro and show notes, not the argument.
items.angle: A concentrated owner-operator naming bear-case risks is the useful part. The email itself has no substance beyond the description, so open the episode.
items.tweetA: The biggest shareholder in 25 junior miners is asked what keeps him up at night. His answer matters more than the thesis, because concentrated owners in illiquid juniors can't hedge with a stop. Gold at $4,160 doesn't remove that.
items.tweetB: Canadian mining is getting political support at the same moment gold is $4,160 and South Korea is buying 1 ton. Juniors are a call option on both, and the tail risk of one is the other reversing.

items.title: South Korea to buy 1 ton of gold (its first purchase in years); China 'weaponising' rare earths; gold at $4,160
items.idea: Mando headlines: South Korea to buy 1 ton of gold, with the text saying the first purchase since 2023 while the link's slug says 2013; US envoy accuses China of 'weaponising' rare earths; China eyes more targeted fiscal support; Nasdaq 100 posted an all-time-high monthly close; gold at $4,160.
items.angle: Check the year on the Korea purchase before quoting. A central-bank bid and a rare-earth dispute are two supports for gold and critical minerals.
items.tweetA: South Korea buys a ton of gold with gold at $4,160, and the 10y at a multi-decade high. Central banks are buying gold into rising real yields. That's not a trade, it's a statement about the dollar.
items.tweetB: A US envoy says China is weaponising rare earths and Korea is rebuilding gold reserves. The two assets countries can't sanction or print are getting stockpiled in the same week.

items.title: McKinsey: build for multiple energy futures and know the signposts, as AI becomes a new source of power demand
items.idea: The teaser says the energy system is becoming 'more uncertain, not less': demand growing, AI creating a new source of power demand, geopolitics reshaping supply chains, and affordability and security alongside decarbonization. McKinsey's advice is to stop betting on a single energy future and instead build for multiple plausible futures, with signposts that trigger a change of course. Webinars on Oct 8 (energy) and Oct 14 (materials).
items.angle: Light on numbers in the email; the full report has the scenarios. Pair with the Amazon-Constellation PPA and diesel items.
items.tweetA: McKinsey says the energy strategy is no longer a single bet, it's a set of signposts. This week's signposts: a 20-year nuclear PPA, $230 diesel, China banning fuel exports. All three are in one inbox.
items.tweetB: AI as a new source of power demand is now a consulting-deck line. The part that isn't in a deck: it's being bought in 20-year contracts by one company at a time.
